hints: Look at the whole cell on the right and find its longest side from top to bottom. Measure that image length in millimetres with a ruler.
Remember magnification links what you measure to the real size: magnification = image size divided by actual size, so rearrange to find actual size and convert mm to micrometres.
walkthrough:
**Measure the image**

Grab a ruler and measure the maximum length of the complete cell on the right. You should get about $73 \text{ mm}$ from the top to the bottom of the cell.

This is your image size. Keep it in mm for now.

**Use the magnification formula**

Magnification tells us how many times bigger the image is than real life. Rearrange it to find the real size:
$$actual\ size = \frac{image\ size}{magnification}$$
$$actual\ size = \frac{73 \text{ mm}}{108\,000}$$

**Calculate and convert to micrometres**

First calculate in mm, then convert to $\mu m$. Remember $1 \text{ mm} = 1000 \text{ } \mu m$:
$$actual\ size = 0.000676 \text{ mm}$$
$$actual\ size = 0.000676 \times 1000 = 0.676 \text{ } \mu m$$
That matches option B, which is a sensible size for a small bacterial cell.

options.A: Too small. This would come from measuring the width across the cell rather than the maximum top to bottom length.
options.B: Correct. An image of about 73 mm divided by 108 000 gives about 0.676 micrometres, the true maximum length.
options.C: Too large, about double the true value. This suggests an error in measuring the image length or in the division.
options.D: Ten times too large. This is the classic unit conversion slip, forgetting that 1 mm equals 1000 micrometres, not 10 000.
